Learning Objectives
Appreciate unique cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurologic responses to pain and surgery
in older adults.
Recognize the importance of rapid stabilization and optimization for early surgical
management.
Perform age- and indication-appropriate preoperative risk assessment.
Provide reasonable estimates of postoperative functional outcomes.
Identify the small number of medical contraindications to urgent surgical fixation.
Discuss methods to limit perioperative hypotension.
Manage common postoperative conditions, including pain, delirium, bleeding, and oliguria.
Prepare patients for facility- or home-based rehabilitation postoperatively.

Relevant Perioperative Physiology in Older Adults
Cardiovascular System
The cardiovascular system stiffens, resulting in labile blood pressure and tachyarrhythmia
under conditions of stress.1 In particular, older adults typically are prone to exaggerated
perioperative hypotension in response to blood loss, anesthesia, and antihypertensive
medications. Specific cardiovascular changes include the following:
Left ventricular hypertrophy and impaired ventricular filling
Elevated atrial pressures
Stiff arterial walls and poorly compliant blood vessels
Pulmonary System
Changes to the pulmonary system result in lower thresholds for dyspnea, hypoxia,
hypercarbia, and aspiration during the perioperative period.2 Specific pulmonary system
changes include the following:
Stiffening of the pulmonary parenchyma, resulting in reduced lung compliance
Neuromuscular aging can produce diaphragmatic and chest wall weakness.
Kyphoscoliosis reduces capacity for ventilation.
Swallowing mechanisms also deteriorate, increasing the likelihood of clinically important
pulmonary aspiration.
Encephalopathy and delirium may transiently limit optimal respiratory dynamics.
Neurocognitive System
Changes to the brain and associated structures3 substantially lower the threshold for delirium
in response to common perioperative conditions, including pain, sleep disturbance,
medications, and environmental changes. Specific changes include the following:
Loss of neurons, decreased synaptic connections, and decreased supporting glial elements
Cerebrovascular changes resulting in impaired autoregulation of cerebral blood flow

Physiologic changes of aging result in perioperative lability in many relevant organs,
including the cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurocognitive systems. In addition, older
adults often experience age-related declines in renal and hepatic function that are not
matched with markedly abnormal laboratory findings but still have considerable effects
on the metabolism and excretion of many common medications. These changes
contribute to the exaggerated clinical effect of pain, medications, blood loss, and
anesthesia on older adults, making older patients more susceptible to minor stimuli and
common clinical events than younger patients. The care team must recognize that
typical tests, treatment options, and medications most commonly used and validated in
younger patient populations may be harmful in older adults and that unique approaches
are necessary to avoid hemodynamic, pulmonary, and neurocognitive complications
during the perioperative period.
Preoperative Management
Preoperative Risk Assessment
The tools and objectives for preoperative risk assessment for urgent and emergent surgical
management are substantially different than those recommended for elective surgical
procedures.
Risk assessments in older adults are unique and are enhanced by measures of functional and
cognitive status and typical comorbidity evaluations.
Preoperative optimization of comorbidities should be managed in an interdisciplinary fashion
to optimize efficiency and value-based care.
Comorbidity assessment
Evaluation of comorbidities in geriatric trauma patients is essential to determining a patient’s
risk profile and identifying risk for complications.
Comorbidities can be classified as chronic-stable, chronic-unstable, and newly diagnosed.
Chronic-stable conditions are unrelated to the trauma but need to be evaluated
preoperatively to maintain the comorbidity in a stable condition.
A chronic-unstable condition may be directly related to the geriatric trauma and must be
evaluated preoperatively to optimize the patient’s medical condition before surgical
treatment can be safely performed.

The most important initial comorbidity assessment is to identify one of the few acute medical
contraindications to surgical fixation.4 These include the following:
Acute coronary syndromes, including unstable myocardial ischemia or infarction
Severe sepsis with hemodynamic instability and/or inadequate source control of infection
Uncontrolled or unstable arrhythmias (rapid atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia,
or heart block)
Decompensated heart failure with clinically important pulmonary edema
Acute cerebrovascular accident
Severe metabolic abnormalities (eg, profound hyponatremia or hyperkalemia)
Other substantial comorbidities that would not typically delay surgical management
Cardiac valve stenosis
Chronic systolic or diastolic heart failure
Acute kidney injury because of blood loss
Stable chronic coronary artery disease
Controlled atrial fibrillation
Chronic renal failure
Advanced dementia
The Charlson Comorbidity Index5 is a validated and widely used tool that can help classify
chronic comorbidities for the purposes of outcome assessment. The Charlson Comorbidity
Index is simple to calculate (many online calculators exist) and has been shown to predict 1-,
5-, and 10-year mortality risk. The Charlson Comorbidity Index comprises 19 comorbid
conditions that are assigned a value of 1 through 6 based on the mortality risk of each illness
(Table 1).

Capturing a patient’s comorbidity profile on admission helps develop a risk profile for the
patient that can be used to guide treatment.
Comorbidities in the Charlson Comorbidity Index can be chronic-stable, chronic-unstable, or
newly diagnosed.
Preoperative Physical Status Assessment
Preoperative physical status assessment is another key component of the preoperative risk
assessment for geriatric trauma patients. Physical status refers to the systemic nature of the
comorbidity.
In general, the physical examination should focus on key areas of preoperative optimization,
including the following:
Identifying any acute cardiac, pulmonary, neurologic, or hemodynamic contraindication to
urgent surgical management
Vital signs assessment
Cardiopulmonary assessment to confirm hemodynamic stability and assess severe
underlying cardiac valve disease
Pulmonary examination to identify substantial pulmonary compromise
Neurologic examination to exclude new acute neurologic injury (eg, stroke, spinal cord
injury)

Preoperative Physical Status Assessment
The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status Classification System is a
widely used and accepted physical status classification system.6 ASA physical status is
classified from 1 to 6, with 1 denoting a normal healthy patient, 2 denoting a patient with
mild systemic disease, 3 denoting a patient with severe systemic disease, 4 denoting a
patient with a severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, 5 denoting a
moribund patient who is not suspected to survive without the surgical procedure, and 6
denoting a brain-dead individual; Table 2 lists specific examples of comorbidities that

Cardiac Risk Assessment
Preoperative cardiac risk assessment guidelines set forth by the American College of
Cardiology/American Heart Association primarily are focused on elective surgical decision
making.7 Patients with typical fragility fractures will not benefit from noninvasive testing
preoperatively; noninvasive testing results in delayed surgical management while not changing
cardiac management. Although these guidelines are not specifically targeted toward trauma
patients requiring urgent or emergent orthopaedic procedures, some elements of the
guidelines may help inform risk assessments.
Preoperative exercise capacity is helpful to determine a patient’s perioperative cardiac risk and
may be useful in urgent or emergent surgical planning. Exercise capacity is a measure of a
patient’s ability to perform routine physical activity without decompensating.
A tool used to stratify exercise tolerance is the metabolic equivalent (MET).8 A MET is the
resting metabolic rate (amount of oxygen consumed at rest) when sitting quietly in a chair—
approximately 3.5 mL O2/kg/min (1.2 kcal/min for a 70-kg individual). This means that work at
2 METs requires twice the metabolism, and so forth. One MET is the ability to perform basic
tasks to take care of oneself, such as eating, dressing, or toileting; 4 METs equates to walking

Patients with good exercise tolerance (METs >4) typically have a good short-term prognosis.
A baseline resting 12-lead electrocardiogram is routinely obtained for all geriatric trauma
patients.
Advanced cardiac testing (echocardiography, stress testing, extended preoperative telemetry)
is only indicated if it will change management before urgent surgical fixation. If patients do not
have an acute cardiac contraindication to surgical treatment (acute coronary syndrome,
unstable arrhythmia, decompensated heart failure, critical valve disease), no additional
preoperative testing typically is warranted.
If preoperative stress testing is performed and is positive, studies have shown no
improvement in outcome if prophylactic revascularization is performed preoperatively.

Preoperative pulmonary risk assessment typically is focused on information obtained during
the patient history and physical examination.
Chest radiography may be considered if signs or symptoms of cardiopulmonary disease are
present; however, it should not be performed routinely.
Functional Status Assessment
Functional status is predictive of perioperative and longer-term recovery outcomes.
Functional status can be quantified via the Barthel Index for Activities of Daily Living.9 This
index assesses patients for dependence in key areas, including feeding, bathing, grooming,
dressing, bowel and bladder continence, toileting, and mobility (Resource 1).
Cognitive Assessment
Pre-fracture cognitive impairment also strongly predicts short- and long-term outcomes.
For patients without a formal diagnosis of dementia, historical clues, including impairments in
telephone use, handling of finances, and inability to self-administer medications, best
correlate with a diagnosis of dementia.10
For patients without delirium, the Mini-Cog test11 can help identify dementia (Resource 2).
Comprehensive Risk Assessment Tools
Validated preoperative risk calculators include the Revised Cardiac Risk Index,12 the
Nottingham Hip Fracture Score,13 (Resource 3), and the American College of Surgeons
National Surgical Quality Improvement Program Surgical Risk Calculator.14
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index is the simplest and most validated tool but is primarily focused
on comorbidity assessment (Resource 4).
Tools that incorporate functional and cognitive elements into risk assessment likely are most
predictive of the full range of important postoperative outcomes and complications and are
increasingly validated for hip fracture populations (Resource 5).
Preoperative Laboratory Testing
Complete blood counts; routine chemistries, including electrolyte levels and renal function;
and assessment of coagulation function for select patients are the only required laboratory

Additional studies related to the workup of metabolic bone disease (albumin, calcium,
phosphorus, and vitamin D levels and thyroid and parathyroid assessment) may be helpful for
secondary fracture prevention.
Core Preoperative Preparation
Correct volume depletion with isotonic intravenous fluid therapy (lactated Ringer solution or
saline)
Withhold antihypertensive medications; discuss optimal dosing with medical team.
Withhold oral diabetes medications and transition to sliding scale insulin.
Withhold diuretic agents.
Ensure adequate preoperative blood volume, typically hemoglobin level10 g/dL or higher.
Pain control with nerve blockade for hip and femoral neck fractures, intravenous opioids
Rapid assessment for contraindications to surgical management
Early fixation to limit ongoing blood loss and pain
Interdisciplinary Patient Care in the Perioperative Setting
The role of interdisciplinary care for geriatric trauma patients has been adopted by the
American College of Surgeons.
According to American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Program Best
Practice Guidelines, preoperative optimization of geriatric trauma patients with considerable
medical comorbidities is recommended to be performed in conjunction with a medical
specialist or a geriatrician (Resource 6).
Co-management of orthopaedic geriatric trauma patients is becoming more common.15 This
concept refers to the practice of admitting patients to the orthopaedic service but having the
consulting medical specialist take co-ownership of the medical care of patients. The medical
consultant often will continue to manage ongoing medical issues.
Co-management of geriatric trauma patients by an orthopaedic surgeon and a geriatrician
has been shown to decrease hospital length of stay, hospital readmission rates, time to
surgery, complication rates, and inpatient mortality rates.
Several specific models for co-management exist based on the resources available.

Interdisciplinary Patient Care in the Perioperative Setting
Preoperative risk assessment and optimization typically are done in parallel for geriatric
patients with a fragility fracture. Hip and femur fractures typically are managed via
urgent surgical treatment to minimize acute decompensation from blood loss and
delirium and to limit the period of perioperative immobility and subsequent muscle loss
and functional decline. Because geriatric patients with a fracture are have more
comorbidities and are more frail than other patients, they cannot tolerate ongoing blood
loss, pain, and immobility and require relatively rapid fracture fixation. Therefore, the
focus of the preoperative period is efficient preparation for surgical management,
documentation of medical comorbidities to anticipate and prevent postoperative
complications, and prevention of iatrogenic harm from the inappropriate addition or
continuation of medications. Although specific preoperative risk estimates may be
helpful, the prognosis of patients who undergo nonsurgical treatment remains dismal,
and surgical repair is indicated in most patients with all but the highest perioperative
risk. Much, but not all, of preoperative care should be delivered via protocols: rapid
intravenous volume restoration, nerve blocks and opioids for pain control, standard
preoperative blood workup, electrocardiography, and imaging studies. The other
essential preoperative component is the involvement of a medical provider committed
to rapid stabilization who is knowledgeable in geriatric physiology and treatment
strategies and cognizant of common perioperative medical issues. Co-management with
a physician who has experience in the inpatient treatment of older adults has been
repeatedly demonstrated to be essential to optimal outcomes and is necessary to
supplement protocolized care with individualized treatment.
Because many fragility fractures occur in the context of pre-fracture functional and
cognitive decline, excellent surgical management is less likely to result in a return to
preinjury functional status, and the surgical team must anticipate the future needs and
prognosis of patients for recovery in this context.
Postoperative Management

Postoperative complications are common, predictable, and often preventable. Prevention and
management of these complications is essential to optimal hospital and longer-term
outcomes. Common postoperative issues include the following:
Typically multifactorial, including anesthesia, blood loss, and as an adverse effect of pain
medications
Standing blood pressure should be assessed periodically to identify standing hypotension.
Continue to withhold all blood pressure medications, except for heart rate controlling
medications (eg, beta blockers and some calcium channel blockers) or blood pressure
medications that have known withdrawal effects (eg, clonidine)
Most patients require 24 hours of intravenous fluid support until the effects of anesthesia
resolve and oral intake improves.
Consider blood transfusion in patients with a hemoglobin level less than8 g/dL or a large
drop from pre-fracture baseline.
Most patients should not have home blood pressure medications restarted during the
postoperative phase. This typically can be deferred to post-discharge follow-up unless the
patient is substantially hypertensive in the hospital.
Home diabetes mellitus medications also should be withheld and should only be slowly
introduced if necessary based on reliable enteral intake with substantially elevated blood
glucose levels.
Pain
Pain may be related to fracture, implant, incision, skin, and soft-tissue injury, or related to
positioning and immobility.
Pain should be evaluated daily via a numeric rating system for cognitively intact patients or via
behavioral observation scoring in patients with cognitive impairment.
Tools to assess and quantify pain in cognitively impaired patients include the Pain Assessment
in Advanced Dementia tool.
Pain management and medication dosing should be protocolized and include the routine
administration of acetaminophen.
As-needed dosing of opioids (eg, 2.5 to 5 mg of oxycodone) is adequate for most frail patients.
Additional dose titration may be necessary for robust or opioid-tolerant patients.
All patients being treated with opioids also should receive laxatives daily.
Blood Loss

Blood loss may continue for several days postoperatively.
Symptomatic findings may include hypotension, presyncope, renal insufficiency, or dyspnea.
Randomized trial data support reserving blood transfusions for patients with a hemoglobin
level less than 8 g/dL, unless considerable symptoms of anemia exist.16
Delirium
Perioperative delirium is associated with an increased risk of mortality, hospital length of stay,
and functional decline.
Delirium is defined as an acute change in mental status characterized by waxing and waning
status of mental alertness. Delirium is common in patients with underlying dementia but also
frequently is observed in patients without known preexisting cognitive impairment.
Delirium is elicited by many factors, including disorganized sleep, pain, infection, dehydration,
medications, urinary retention, constipation, hypoxia, electrolyte abnormalities, and
hypoglycemia.
The diagnosis and monitoring of delirium are best done via a short four-criteria rule called the
Confusion Assessment Method.17 Patients must have two essential criteria (acute onset and
inattention) and one of two additional criteria (disorganized thinking or altered level of
consciousness) to be classified as delirious (Resource 7).
Delirium may be further characterized as hyperactive (agitated), hypoactive (somnolent), or
mixed.
Prevention and management for delirium is primarily focused on addressing the etiology;
providing a supportive, safe, and less intense medical environment; managing pain,
constipation, and urinary retention; and promoting sleep. In delirious patients, aggravating
treatment options should be stopped if they are no longer medically necessary (eg,
intravenous fluids, telemetry, urinary catheters, oxygen), with clinically appropriate titrations
or cessation of contributing medications.18
For severe agitation, 0.5 mg of haloperidol can be administered as necessary for patients
without contraindications.
Aspiration
Postoperative pulmonary complications are common.
Asymptomatic mild hypoxia may be related to recumbency, atelectasis, and
hypoventilation/sedation.

Aspiration related to anesthesia or sedation may result in tachypnea, fever, and lung findings.
Quick resolution suggests chemical pneumonitis rather than bacterial pneumonia.
Pneumonia can present from postoperative day zero to five and is associated with fever and
new infiltrates observed on chest radiographs.
Preexisting dysphagia is common, and aspiration also can occur during the postoperative
phase.
Prevention of pulmonary complications includes early mobility, coughing and deep breathing,
incentive spirometry, and careful feeding.
Constipation
Commonly observed on admission and often can be appreciated on routine imaging studies
obtained to assess for hip or pelvis fractures
Often results in anorexia, nausea, delirium; fecal impaction may contribute to urinary
retention.
Many common risk factors, including age, immobility, opioids, and other medications
All patients should be treated with routine laxatives, including a stimulant (eg, senna) and/or
osmotic agent (eg, polyethylene glycol).
Oliguria
Bladder scanning can help establish urinary retention.
Oliguria that persists more than 1 or 2 days postoperatively is less likely the result of volume
depletion and more likely to the result of other factors, such as urinary retention, renal failure,
or diuretic agent dependence.
Volume Overload
Perioperative volume overload contributors include intravenous fluids and temporarily
cessation of diuretic agents.
May lead to considerable soft-tissue and pulmonary edema
Daily weight gain may help identify substantial volume overload prior to symptoms.
Home diuretic agents can be resumed after postoperative bleeding has stopped and patient is
taking oral fluids.


Volume Overload
Optimal postoperative management is facilitated by a thorough understanding of typical
responses to anesthesia and blood loss and close attention to specific patient
comorbidities. The early postoperative period is dominated by resolving vasodilation,
anesthesia effects, and blood loss. In general during the first one or two days
postopertively, patients require additional intravascular volume support via intravenous
fluids; should not be receiving home diuretic agents or antihypertensive medications;
and require close monitoring for aspiration events, respiratory failure, and delirium. By
postoperative day two, most patients have completed the transition from this acute
phase and have a new baseline of blood pressure, function, and exercise tolerance
because of blood loss and muscle catabolism during the perioperative period. Even after
the recovery of mental status and the stability of blood counts, geriatric patients are
unlikely to tolerate their previous level of exertion or many of their home
antihypertensive or diabetic medications. Therefore, home medications that the patient
has tolerated for years may need to be carefully reintroduced, if at all, and closely
titrated to the new postoperative physiology of the patient. Close co-management with a
medicine provider who is experienced in perioperative and geriatric physiology is
necessary for optimal outcomes.
